background.title: How Paper 1 answers are marked
background.html:
Psychology exams have no multiple choice. You write answers, and examiners mark them with markbands: short descriptions of what an answer at each level looks like. For a 4-mark question there are two bands, 1-2 marks and 3-4 marks.

The first word of the question, the command term, says what kind of answer gets the top band. Describe means give a detailed account. Explain means a detailed account plus reasons or causes. Answering "describe" when the question says "explain" keeps you in the lower band, even if every sentence is true.

background.title: Two kinds of learning you met in session 2
background.html:
Classical conditioning: learning by linking two things that happen together. Pavlov's dogs drooled at a sound that always came just before food.

Operant conditioning: learning from what happens after you do something. A behaviour that is rewarded (reinforced) happens more; a behaviour that is punished happens less.

In both, the learner experiences things directly. Today's social learning theory adds a third way: learning by watching other people and what happens to them.

background.title: What a theory and a model are
background.html:
A theory is an explanation of why or how something happens, which can be checked against evidence.

A model is a simplified picture of how something works, often drawn as boxes and arrows, like a map of the underground: it leaves out details so you can see the main route.

Neither is ever "proven". Researchers use them to make predictions ("if this is true, then people should forget a word within 20 seconds"), then run studies to see whether the predictions come true. Studies that fit support the model; studies that do not fit show it needs changing.

background.title: Memory in everyday words: in, kept, out
background.html:
Every memory has three steps:

  • In: you notice something and take it in, for example a new classmate's name.
  • Kept: it is stored, for a few seconds or for years.
  • Out: you get it back when you need it, for example when you see her the next day. Getting it back is called retrieval.

Forgetting can happen at any step: you never really noticed, it was not kept, or you cannot find it when you need it (the name is "on the tip of your tongue").

background.title: Averages and putting numbers in order
background.html:
An average is one number that sums up a whole set of numbers. Psychology uses three:

  • Mean: add them all and divide by how many. Scores 4, 6 and 8: 18 ÷ 3 = 6.
  • Median: write them in order from smallest to largest and take the middle one. For 3, 9, 5 that is 3, 5, 9, so the median is 5.
  • Mode: the one that appears most often. In 2, 3, 3, 7 the mode is 3.

Always sort the numbers first when you need the median.

background.title: Percentages and milliseconds
background.html:
A percentage is "out of 100". 80% recalled means 80 out of every 100 items were remembered; under 10% means fewer than 10 out of 100.

A millisecond (ms) is one thousandth of a second. Reaction times are often around 400 to 500 ms: just under half a second. 1 240 ms is about one and a quarter seconds, which is very slow for a simple reaction task.

terms.def: In IB Psychology, one of three ways of explaining behaviour: biological (body and brain), cognitive (thinking and memory) or sociocultural (other people and culture).
To do with other people, groups and culture. The sociocultural approach explains behaviour through the people around us.
To do with thinking: paying attention, remembering, deciding. The cognitive approach explains behaviour through what goes on in the mind.
In this course, one of four real-life areas where psychology is used, such as learning and cognition, or health and well-being.
A level on the examiners' marking grid, such as 1-2 marks or 3-4 marks. Each band describes what an answer must contain to get those marks.
The examiners' guide to marking a paper: what earns marks and what does not.
A sample exam made by the IB to show what the real papers for this course will look like.
IB command term: "Give a detailed account." Say what something is or what happened, with detail. No reasons needed.
IB command term: "Give a detailed account including reasons or causes." Describe, then say why or how.
Made up for the purpose of an example, but realistic. "Imagine a teacher gives a merit point..." is a hypothetical example.
Anything in the surroundings that a person or animal can sense and react to: a sound, a smell, food, a picture.
Unconditioned means natural, not learned (drooling at food). Conditioned means learned (drooling at a sound that has been linked with food).
Learning from consequences: a behaviour that is followed by a reward happens more often, and one followed by punishment happens less often.
Adding something pleasant, such as praise or a merit point, straight after a behaviour, so the behaviour happens more often.
When a learned behaviour fades away because the link or the reward that kept it going has stopped.
A device that makes a regular ticking sound, used by musicians to keep time.
Experienced through someone else. Vicarious reinforcement: you see someone else rewarded, and that makes you more likely to do the same.
Learning by watching another person (the model) and later copying what they did.
Feeling that a model is like you, for example the same age or gender. We copy people we identify with more.
Keeping something in memory. In social learning theory: remembering what the model did well enough to copy it later.
Your belief that you can succeed at a particular task. High self-efficacy makes you more likely to try.
Behaviour meant to hurt or harm someone or something, by hitting, kicking or hurtful words.
A large inflatable toy clown that springs back up when hit. Bandura used it to see whether children would copy an adult hitting it.
A person with many followers on social media whose posts can affect what followers buy, eat or do.
An explanation of why or how something happens, which can be tested against evidence.
A simplified picture, often boxes and arrows, of how a mental process such as memory works, used to make predictions that studies can test.
Based on real observation or measurement, not on opinion or pure reasoning.
State exactly how something will be measured, so anyone could do it the same way. "Memory" becomes "number of trigrams recalled after 18 seconds".
An idea you cannot see or touch directly, such as memory or intelligence. It must be turned into something measurable first.
A framework is a basic structure of ideas. A representation is something that stands for something else, like a map stands for a city.
A clear, testable prediction of what a study will find.
How much something can hold. The capacity of short-term memory is how many items it can hold at once.
How long something lasts.
In the multi-store model, a separate place or system where information is held: sensory memory, short-term memory or long-term memory.
Going over information again in your head. Maintenance rehearsal is just repeating it; elaborative rehearsal is thinking about what it means.
Grouping separate items into bigger meaningful units so you can hold more at once: 1, 9, 4, 5 becomes the year 1945.
Two ways of losing information from short-term memory. Decay: it fades with time. Displacement: new items push old ones out because there is little room.
A group of three letters with no meaning, such as TGH, used so that people cannot link it to anything they already know.
When people learn a list, they remember the first items and the last items better than those in the middle.
Three kinds of processing a word. Structural: how it looks. Phonetic: how it sounds. Semantic: what it means.
A memory test where you pick out items you saw before from a longer list, instead of recalling them from nothing.
How well a study's task and setting match real life. Learning lists of nonsense letters is not much like everyday memory, so ecological validity is low.
Skills of body movement, such as riding a bike or drawing, that improve with practice.
Information collected in a study: numbers such as scores, or words such as interview answers.
Numbers that sum up a set of data, such as an average or how spread out the scores are.
One number that describes the typical or middle value of a set of data: the mean, the median or the mode.
How spread out a set of data is. The range (largest minus smallest) is the simplest measure. Coming in a later lesson.
Two measures of how spread out data are, which you will learn in a later HL lesson. Not needed today.
Data that are just names of categories with no order, such as favourite colour.
Data that can be put in order, but the gaps between steps are not equal, such as mild, moderate, severe.
Data with equal steps but no true zero, such as temperature in degrees Celsius.
Data with equal steps and a true zero, where 0 means none at all, such as reaction time or number of words recalled.
A value far away from all the others in a data set, such as one reaction time of 1 240 ms when the rest are around 420 ms.
When a graph of the data is lopsided, with a long tail on one side. Positively skewed: a few very high values make a long tail on the right.
Symmetrical: the same on both sides of the middle, like a mirror image. Asymmetrical: not the same on both sides.
How the values in a data set are spread out, usually seen as the shape of a bar graph of how often each value occurs.
The HL-only exam (1 h 45, 30% of your grade) where you analyse graphs, tables and research findings.
Analyse: break something down to show its main parts. Interpret: work out what data or results mean and what conclusion they support.
Intelligence quotient: a score from an intelligence test, where 100 is average.
Latin for "and others". "Coates et al." means Coates and the other researchers who wrote the study.
A person who takes part in a study.
Being successful at something through your own effort. Mastery experiences are your own past successes.
Other people telling you that you can do something, which makes you try harder.
Weighing up strengths and limitations, then giving a judgement. A "describe" or "explain" question does not ask for it.
